newsitem.title: FRANCE: France buries hatchet with Italy over lira.
newsitem.headline: France buries hatchet with Italy over lira.

text.p: France appears to have buried the hatchet with Italy in a row over the devaluation of the lira four years ago by backing the weekend re-entry of Italian currency into the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

Indeed, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis went out of his way to suggest France had shown some sympathy for Italy's position at Brussels talks on the lira's re-entry to the ERM, scotching earlier reports that described Paris as Rome's main opponent.

The decision to let the lira back into the ERM at a central rate of 990 per mark follows years of sniping by Paris that Italy had benefitted from a "competitive devaluation" when its currency was forced out of the ERM in a 1992 currency crisis.

Official sources said France's support for Italy's ERM membership reflected its desire to see as many countries as possible join European monetary union in 1999, provided they met Maastricht treaty criteria.
Two-year membership of the ERM is seen by most officials as a requirement in order to qualify for monetary union.
"The European Monetary System is the antechamber for the euro," Arthuis told reporters.
He suggested that France had been prepared to support a rate of 298 lira per franc, equivalent to the 1,000 lira per mark which Italians were seeking, in order to get an agreement,
"France thought 298 lira per franc was fair," he said.
In the end EU ministers agreed to bring the lira back into the ERM at 295 lira per franc, or 990 per mark.

Sources at the talks said Germany, rather than France, had been the key opponent of a weaker lira parity during the talks, which dragged on for two days over Italian insistence that the central ERM rate should not below 1,000 per mark.

Economists said while Arthuis's remarks did not necessarily tie in with France's previous call for a rise in the lira, nor indeed with other comments from official sources, they nonetheless indicated a willingness to build bridges with Italy -- at least in its public statements.
French President Jacques Chirac provoked a diplomatic row with Italy in October by saying that Italy might not be fit to join monetary union in 1999.
"I think Arthuis's stance was trying to lay a little bit of that to rest," UBS economist Darren Williams said.

Chirac calmed the row at an October 4 summit in Naples backing Italy's aim to rejoin the ERM, though an official source said it would be wrong to think France and Italy reached a deal on the lira's ERM entry level at those talks.

France's determinedly constructive approach to Italy comes at a time when its relationship with its main partner Germany appears to be under strain over exchange rate policy for the future euro and over German proposals for an EU stability pact.

France, which has called repeatedly for a strong dollar, appears to have little sympathy in Germany for any exchange rate policy which would deliberately make the new euro weaker than the mark now is.

In an article on Sunday in weekly Journal du Dimanche, Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean Boissonnat acknowledged that tension, saying that "French and Germans need to agree -- between themselves and with their partners -- on how to manage the future euro."
"The French need to understand that the Germans are giving up the mark, which has been very successful for them, without being sure about the stability of the euro," he said.

"And the Germans need to understand French people who do not want rigid and automatic sanctions to manage the new currency without taking into account countries' individual situations at any particular moment," he said.

France has opposed Germany's call for automatic sanctions on countries which run excessive budget deficits after the launch of monetary union, unless these allow some flexibility to take account of special circumstances and for differences in the way these would affect different countries.
